title: A smooth closed subgroup with full tangent space equals a connected algebraic group
statement: Let $k$ be any field [def-weil-field]. Let $A$ be an affine $k$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], connected in the underlying topological space [def-weil-connected-scheme], and let $j:B\hookrightarrow A$ be a closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Suppose $B$ is smooth over $k$ [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Write $\operatorname{Lie}(J)=T_{J/k,e_J}$ for the tangent space at the identity of $J$ [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space]. If $dj_e:\operatorname{Lie}(B)\to\operatorname{Lie}(A)$ is surjective, then $j$ is an isomorphism of $k$-group schemes. There is no hypothesis on the characteristic or perfectness of $k$, and no connectedness hypothesis on $B$ or smoothness hypothesis on $A$.

source.place: Proposition 10.15, printed pp.190-191, including its proof; arbitrary ground field, smooth closed subgroup, connected ambient algebraic group.

proof.text: Write $A=\operatorname{Spec}C$. By the affine description of a closed immersion, $B=\operatorname{Spec}(C/I)$ for an ideal $I\subset C$. The algebra $C$ is finite type over $k$, hence so is $C/I$ (the images of any finite algebra-generating set generate the quotient). In particular $B$ is an affine group scheme of finite type. Both identity points have residue field $k$: their maps to $\operatorname{Spec}k$ have the identity sections as rational points. The rings $C$ and $C/I$ are Noetherian, since a field has just the ideals $0,k$ and finite-type algebras over a Noetherian ring are Noetherian. The local rings $R_J=\mathcal O_{J,e_J}$, for $J=A,B$, are their localizations at the identity primes and are therefore Noetherian local rings.

source.place: Proposition 10.15, pp.190-191: finite-type closed subgroup setting; Proposition 1.37 and its rational-identity local-ring proof, p.18. Supporting algebra: Stacks Tags 01QO, 01T2, 00FN, 01HV.

proof.text: For $J=A,B$, put $Q_J=\mathfrak m_{R_J}/\mathfrak m_{R_J}^2$. The Noetherian local cotangent-dimension theorem says that $Q_J$ is finite dimensional and $\dim R_J\leq\dim_k Q_J$, with equality precisely when $R_J$ is regular. Rational tangent-cotangent duality identifies $T_{J/k,e_J}$ with $Q_J^*$. Finite-dimensional duality gives $\dim_k Q_J^*=\dim_k Q_J$; write this common finite integer as $t_J$. Finally the group identity-local-dimension theorem gives $d_J:=\dim J=\dim R_J$. Thus $d_J\leq t_J$, and $d_J=t_J$ if and only if $R_J$ is regular. All dimensions here are finite nonnegative integers; nonemptiness follows from the identity section.

source.place: Proposition 1.37, p.18, and the dimension paragraph after 1.36, p.17, as used in the first sentence of the proof of 10.15. Local ingredients: Stacks Tags 00KU, 0B2E.

proof.text: Since $B\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth and affine, the ring map $k\to C/I$ is smooth. Every localization of a smooth algebra over a field at a prime is regular. In particular $R_B$ is regular, so step 2 gives $d_B=t_B$. This argument requires neither connectedness of $B$ nor any restriction on $k$.

source.place: Proposition 10.15, p.191: the equality dim(H)=dim(h); Proposition 1.37, p.18. Affine smoothness and regularity: Stacks Tags 02H6, 01V6, 00TT.

proof.text:
Surjectivity of $dj_e$ implies $t_A\leq t_B$: lift a basis of $T_{A/k,e_A}$ to $T_{B/k,e_B}$; any relation between the lifts maps to a relation between that basis, so the lifts are independent. Also $d_B\leq d_A$, because the closed embedding $|B|\hookrightarrow|A|$ sends every strict chain of irreducible closed subsets to a strict chain of the same length. Combining these two elementary comparisons with steps 2 and 3 yields
$$d_B=t_B\ \geq\ t_A\ \geq\ d_A\ \geq\ d_B.$$
All entries are therefore equal. In particular $d_A=t_A$, $R_A$ is regular by step 2, and $d_A=d_B$.

source.place: Proposition 10.15, p.191: the displayed dimension chain. Surjectivity suffices for the first comparison; tangent injectivity is not needed.

proof.text: The regular ring $R_A$ is the localization of the finite-type algebra $C$ at its identity prime. Its residue field is $k$, a finite separable extension of itself. The regular-separable smooth-neighbourhood theorem therefore supplies a smooth open neighbourhood of $e_A$ in $A$. Apply the group smoothness-at-identity criterion over $S=\operatorname{Spec}k$: this base is locally Noetherian (a field has only two ideals), and $A\to S$ is flat, since every $k$-module is flat and flatness is checked on affine charts. The group is of finite type by hypothesis. The criterion now implies that $A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth at every point, hence smooth. The separability used here is solely that of $k/k$, not perfectness of $k$.

source.place: Proposition 10.15, p.191: equality forces G smooth, using 1.37 and Proposition 1.28, printed p.14. Rational-point smoothness: Stacks Tag 00TV (lemma-separable-smooth).

proof.text: The smoothness of the affine scheme $A$ makes $C$ a smooth $k$-algebra. Hence every local ring of $A$ at a closed point is regular, and $C$ is reduced. The smooth-components-disjoint theorem applies to this affine finite-type scheme and says that its finitely many irreducible components are its connected components. Since $A$ is connected, there is only one such component, so $A$ is irreducible. We have thus obtained an irreducible reduced affine finite-type scheme over the original field $k$.

source.place: Proposition 10.15, p.191, final parenthesis (G smooth and connected); compare Corollary 1.35, p.17. Supporting regularity and reducedness: Stacks Tags 00TT, 056T.

proof.text: The image $Y=j(|B|)$ is a closed subset of the irreducible affine variety $A$, with coordinate algebra $C$ (finitely generated by step 1 and reduced by step 6). If it were proper, the affine dimension-drop theorem would give $\dim Y<\dim C$, where both sides are lengths of chains of primes of the coordinate algebras $C$ and $C/\mathfrak a$, $\mathfrak a$ the radical ideal with $V(\mathfrak a)=Y$. By the comparison of the Krull dimension of a ring with the topological Krull dimension of its spectrum, $\dim C=d_A$, and $\dim C/\mathfrak a$ is the topological dimension of $\operatorname{Spec}C/\mathfrak a$, which is homeomorphic to the subspace $V(\mathfrak a)=Y$ of $\operatorname{Spec}C$; so $\dim Y<d_A$ in the topological sense. But a closed immersion is a homeomorphism onto its image, so $\dim j(|B|)=d_B=d_A$ by step 4, a contradiction. Thus $j(|B|)=|A|$.

source.place: Proposition 10.15, p.191, final inference dim(G)=dim(H) implies G=H; strict dimension drop for a proper closed subset.

proof.text: Apply the reduced-source factorization theorem to $\operatorname{id}_A:A\to A$ and $j:B\hookrightarrow A$. The source $A$ is reduced: by step 6 the ring $C$ is reduced, and each local ring $\mathcal O_{A,x}$ is a localization of $C$ by the affine-open stalk description, and a localization of a reduced ring is reduced (if $(r/s)^n=0$ then $tr^n=0$ for some $t\notin\mathfrak p_x$, so $(tr)^n=0$, $tr=0$ and $r/s=0$). Its image is contained in $j(|B|)$ by step 7. We obtain $s:A\to B$ with $j\circ s=\operatorname{id}_A$. In the affine quotient description from step 1, this gives a left inverse to $C\twoheadrightarrow C/I$, which is consequently injective as well as surjective. Hence $I=0$ and $j$ is an isomorphism of $k$-schemes. Its inverse respects multiplication, identity and inverse: compose each required equality with the isomorphism $j$ and use the corresponding compatibility for $j$. It is therefore an isomorphism of $k$-group schemes.

source.place: Proposition 10.15, p.191, scheme-theoretic conclusion; Milne A.30 (reduced-source factorization), also Stacks Tag 0356.
